doctrine:
**Civil liability arising from a source other than the delict (law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict under Article 1157 of the Civil Code) may be adjudged in the same criminal action even if the accused is acquitted**, despite the limitation in Rule 111, Section 1(a) of the Rules of Court, and without violating due process. "For uniformity," the Court **laid down new parameters**: the award may be made in the criminal action subject to the following conditions:

- (1) the act or omission complained of in the criminal action is the same as or is related to the act or omission giving rise to the civil liability;
- (2) the civil liability of the accused was raised in the criminal action;
- (3) the accused was given the opportunity to be heard on this point; and
- (4) the civil liability of the accused was established by a preponderance of evidence.

The Court based this on Article 29 of the Civil Code and Rule 120, Section 2 (a judgment of acquittal "shall determine if the act or omission from which the civil liability might arise did not exist"), and **reaffirmed the En Banc ruling in *Padilla v. Court of Appeals*** that courts may adjudge civil liability in the same criminal case where the acquittal is pronounced. Division rulings holding otherwise cannot overturn an En Banc doctrine (Article VIII, Section 4(3), Constitution). Because the civil action is deemed instituted with the criminal action, the accused is expected to present there all defenses on the civil aspect.

Reiterated: (a) **Other Deceits under Article 318, paragraph 1 of the RPC** requires a false pretense or fraudulent act made **prior to or simultaneously with** the fraud, which must be the very cause or only motive for the offended party to part with his property. There is no fraudulent concealment of a mortgage that the lender admitted seeing annotated on the titles, and acts done after the transaction cannot supply the deceit. (b) Under *Gomez v. People*, which abandoned *Quisay v. People*, the lack of the prior written authority or approval of the provincial, city or chief state prosecutor on the Information does not divest the trial court of jurisdiction.
facts:
Spouses Enrique and Marites Llonillo, through their agent Grace Pangan, offered private complainant Pedro Joel Caspillo a *sangla-tira* arrangement over apartment units in their two buildings at 236 Aguho Street, Barangay Comembo, Makati City: the lender would lend them money for a fixed period and, as interest, collect the PHP 10,000.00 monthly rent of a unit. According to the prosecution, they assured Caspillo the properties had no liens or encumbrances and showed him the TCTs. On March 30, 2009, Caspillo lent them PHP 300,000.00 and chose the then-vacant unit H. A Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) acknowledged receipt of the money, payable on or before March 20, 2010; the interest arrangement was not written in it because Caspillo himself occupied the unit.

Caspillo later leased unit H to a friend for a month, then ran an unprofitable mini store there. Marites offered to find a lessee and assured him of the PHP 10,000.00 monthly rental. The unit was occupied, but Caspillo could not collect the rent. He discovered that the spouses had entered into *sangla-tira* arrangements over the same unit with its occupants, Germalyn Josol and Rodrigo Arevalo, Jr., and that the properties were mortgaged to different banks. The period to pay the PHP 300,000.00 lapsed without payment. An Information dated December 17, 2012 charged the spouses with estafa under Article 318 (Other Deceits) of the RPC before the MeTC of Makati City.

The spouses said it was a simple loan brokered by Grace, that Marites received only PHP 285,000.00, and that they never represented the property as unencumbered. Marites explained that the property was mortgaged to banks to finance construction, was foreclosed by PS Bank after business reverses (including typhoon Ondoy), and was redeemed around March 2012. During trial they sought dismissal because the Information lacked the approval of the city prosecutor, citing Rule 112, Section 4 and *Quisay v. People*; the MeTC denied this on August 4, 2015.

On December 9, 2015, the MeTC convicted the spouses of Other Deceits, sentenced them to six months' imprisonment and a fine of PHP 300,000.00, and ordered them to pay Caspillo PHP 300,000.00 as actual damages with 6% interest from April 10, 2013, plus PHP 30,000.00 as attorney's fees. It found misrepresentation in their subjecting unit H to *sangla-tira* with other persons. The RTC affirmed on April 27, 2016 and the CA affirmed on July 30, 2018 (reconsideration denied April 15, 2019), both stressing the nondisclosure of the prior mortgages. The spouses filed a Rule 45 petition.
issues: Whether the MeTC had jurisdiction to hear, try, and decide the case although the Information did not bear the prior written authority or approval of the city prosecutor.
Whether spouses Llonillo are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of Other Deceits under Article 318, paragraph 1 of the Revised Penal Code.
Whether, despite their acquittal, spouses Llonillo may be held civilly liable in the same criminal action for the unpaid PHP 300,000.00 loan, a liability arising from a source other than the crime.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the MeTC had jurisdiction.** The spouses relied on *Quisay*, but that doctrine was abandoned in *Gomez v. People* (En Banc). Under *Gomez*, the handling prosecutor's authority "has no connection to the trial court's power to hear and decide a case"; the requirement of prior written authority or approval may be waived by the accused through silence, acquiescence, or failure to raise it during arraignment or before entering a plea, and the deficiency "is merely formal and can be cured at any stage of the proceedings." It is sufficient that the resolution of the investigating prosecutor recommending the filing of the Information bears the imprimatur of the provincial, city or chief state prosecutor.

**2. No, they are not guilty.** Guilt is a question of fact not ordinarily reviewed under Rule 45, but the Court took up the facts because the judgment was based on a misapprehension of facts (the fourth recognized exception). Article 318 is a catch-all for deceits not covered by Articles 315 to 317, with three elements: (a) a false pretense, fraudulent act or pretense other than those in Articles 315, 316 and 317; (b) made or executed prior to or simultaneously with the commission of the fraud; and (c) resulting damage or prejudice. False pretense is "an intentional false statement concerning a material matter of fact," and suppression of a material fact that a party is bound in good faith to disclose is equivalent to a false representation (*Marcos v. People*; *Guinhawa v. People*). The false statement must be the very cause or the only motive for the complainant to part with his property.

**There was no suppression of the bank mortgages.** On cross-examination Caspillo admitted that, before the loan, he was shown copies of the two titles, that the mortgage to a financial institution was annotated on them, and that he saw it. Judicial admissions are conclusive and binding unless shown to have been made through palpable mistake or not to have been made at all; neither was shown, so the admission prevails over his assertion that he did not read the annotations because they were negotiating hurriedly. **Nor were the other *sangla-tira* deals made prior to or simultaneously with the fraud:** when the MOA was signed in 2009, unit H was under *sangla-tira* to no one but Caspillo; the deals with Arevalo, Jr. and Josol came only in 2011 and 2012. The first two elements were absent. Damage, however, existed because the loan remained unpaid, so there was still "an act from which civil liability might arise: the act of loaning PHP 300,000.00 and not timely paying it back despite demand."

**3. Yes, civil liability based on contract may be adjudged in the same criminal action.** Article 29 of the Civil Code does not prohibit a judgment of acquittal and an award of damages in the same criminal action, and Rule 120, Section 2 requires a judgment of acquittal to "determine if the act or omission from which the civil liability might arise did not exist." Under Rule 111, Section 2, the civil action based on delict is extinguished only if the final judgment finds that the act or omission from which it may arise did not exist (*De Guzman v. Alvia*). *Padilla v. Court of Appeals* (En Banc) allows courts to adjudge civil liability in the same case where the acquittal is pronounced, and **since *Padilla* is an En Banc decision, later Division decisions holding otherwise cannot overturn it** (Article VIII, Section 4(3), Constitution). With an acquittal, Article 29 contemplates liability from sources independent of the delict, i.e., law, contracts, quasi-contracts and quasi-delicts under Article 1157 (*De Leon, Jr. v. Roqson Industrial Sales, Inc.*), as illustrated in *Sapiera*, *Chiok* and *Horca* (contract) and *Manantan* and *Lumantas* (quasi-delict). Acquittal does not bar the civil aspect where (1) the acquittal is based on reasonable doubt; (2) the decision declares the liability only civil; or (3) the civil liability is not derived from the criminal act.

Hence, **despite the limitation in Rule 111, Section 1(a), civil liability from sources other than the delict may be adjudged in the criminal action if the act or omission complained of is the same as or related to the act or omission giving rise to the civil liability, and this does not violate due process.** Absent waiver, reservation or prior institution of the civil action, the accused is presumed to know that the civil action is deemed instituted with the criminal action, and must present all defenses against restitution, reparation and indemnification (*First Producers Holdings Corp. v. Co*; *Sabandal v. Tongco*). The prosecution proves both guilt and civil liability, and after an acquittal either party may appeal the civil aspect (*Salazar v. People*). The Court then laid down the four conditions stated in the Doctrine.

**All four conditions were met.** The source of the obligation is contract, the MOA. (1) The acts complained of were allegedly done to enable the spouses to borrow the PHP 300,000.00, and nonpayment of that loan was the damage caused, so the loan is related to the acts charged. (2) and (3) The debt was raised in the criminal action: the spouses admitted the loan, and Marites claimed payment but admitted she had no documentary proof. They had every opportunity to prove payment but never did. (4) Having admitted the loan without proof of payment, the evidence tilts in Caspillo's favor. They are liable for PHP 300,000.00 with interest at 12% per annum from April 10, 2013 (filing of the case in court) to June 30, 2013, 6% per annum from July 1, 2013 until finality, and 6% per annum on the total from finality until full payment.
disposition: The Petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated July 30, 2018 and Resolution dated April 15, 2019 in CA-G.R. CR No. 38855 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE, and spouses Enrique and Marites Llonillo were ACQUITTED of Other Deceits under the first paragraph of Article 318 of the RPC. They were held liable to pay Pedro Joel Caspillo the principal amount of PHP 300,000.00, plus legal interest of 12% per annum from April 10, 2013 until June 30, 2013, and 6% per annum from July 1, 2013 until finality of the Decision; the total amount due earns 6% per annum from finality until full payment.

bar_questions.q: Bea lent Carlo PHP 500,000.00 under a written agreement in which Carlo promised to pay on or before June 1, 2023. When Carlo did not pay, he was charged with estafa for allegedly misrepresenting, when he obtained the loan, that he owned the land he offered as security. Bea did not waive, reserve, or separately file the civil action. At trial Carlo admitted the loan and claimed he had paid it, but presented no receipt. The court acquitted Carlo because the alleged false pretense was not proved, but ordered him to pay Bea PHP 500,000.00 plus legal interest as an obligation arising from their loan agreement. Carlo appeals the civil award, arguing that under Rule 111 only the civil liability arising from the offense charged is deemed instituted with the criminal action, and that holding him liable on the contract in a criminal case violates due process. Is Carlo correct?

alac.answer: No. The court may adjudge Carlo's contractual liability for the loan in the same criminal action despite his acquittal.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 29 of the Civil Code and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Court, a judgment of acquittal does not preclude an award of civil liability in the same criminal action. In Spouses Llonillo v. People (G.R. No. 246787, January 30, 2024), the Court En Banc, reaffirming Padilla v. Court of Appeals, held that despite the limitation in Rule 111, Section 1(a), civil liability arising from sources other than the delict (law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict) may be awarded in the criminal action if: (1) the act or omission complained of is the same as or related to the act or omission giving rise to the civil liability; (2) the civil liability was raised in the criminal action; (3) the accused was given the opportunity to be heard on it; and (4) it was established by a preponderance of evidence. Since the civil action is deemed instituted with the criminal action, the accused must already present all defenses on the civil aspect, so there is no denial of due process.
alac.application: Carlo's alleged deceit was committed to obtain the PHP 500,000.00 loan, and the unpaid loan is the damage charged, so his contractual obligation is related to the act complained of. The loan was put in issue in the criminal case, and Carlo was heard on it: he admitted the loan and claimed payment. Having admitted the debt without any proof of payment, his liability is established by a preponderance of evidence. The acquittal rested on the absence of a false pretense, not on a finding that the act from which civil liability might arise, the unpaid loan, did not exist.
alac.conclusion: Carlo is not correct; the award of the unpaid loan with interest in the criminal case is proper.

bar_questions.q: Dina was charged with Other Deceits under Article 318 of the RPC for allegedly concealing a bank mortgage when she obtained a PHP 250,000.00 loan from Ella. Ella did not reserve the civil action. During trial, over Dina's objection, Ella also testified that Dina owed her PHP 120,000.00 for catering services at Dina's wedding in 2019, an obligation not mentioned in the complaint-affidavit or the Information. The court acquitted Dina, found that the PHP 250,000.00 loan had been fully paid, and ordered Dina to pay Ella PHP 120,000.00 for the catering services, which it found proved by a preponderance of evidence. Is the award of PHP 120,000.00 in the criminal case proper?

alac.answer: No. The catering debt cannot be adjudged in the criminal case because it is not related to the act or omission complained of.
alac.legal_basis: Civil liability from sources other than the delict may be adjudged in the criminal action despite an acquittal only if (1) the act or omission complained of in the criminal action is the same as or related to the act or omission giving rise to the civil liability; (2) the civil liability was raised in the criminal action; (3) the accused was given the opportunity to be heard on it; and (4) it was established by a preponderance of evidence. The Court stressed that the civil liability adjudged in criminal proceedings "must be related to the same act or omission complained of in the criminal charge," although it need not be legally sourced from the crime. (Spouses Llonillo v. People, G.R. No. 246787, January 30, 2024)
alac.application: The act charged against Dina is the alleged concealment of a mortgage to obtain the PHP 250,000.00 loan. The catering debt arises from a separate contract made at a different time for a different purpose, and has nothing to do with the alleged deceit or the loan. The first condition is therefore absent, and proof of the debt by a preponderance of evidence does not cure it. The related obligation, the loan, was found fully paid, so nothing related to the charge remains to be awarded.
alac.conclusion: The award of PHP 120,000.00 is improper; Ella must recover the catering debt in a separate civil action.

bar_questions.q: Fely and Gino offered Hector a sangla-tira deal: Hector would lend them PHP 200,000.00 and, as interest, collect the rent of their apartment unit until they paid. Before signing, they showed Hector copies of their titles, on which a bank mortgage was annotated. At their trial for Other Deceits under Article 318 of the RPC, Hector admitted on cross-examination that he saw the mortgage annotation before lending the money, but on redirect he claimed he did not really read it because they were in a hurry. It was also proved that a year after the loan, Fely and Gino gave the same unit under another sangla-tira to Ivan, so Hector could no longer collect the rent, and the loan remains unpaid. (a) Are Fely and Gino guilty of Other Deceits? (b) What is the effect of Hector's statement on cross-examination?

alac.answer: (a) No. The deceit required by Article 318 was not proved. (b) Hector's statement on cross-examination is a judicial admission that binds him and prevails over his later claim that he did not read the annotation.
alac.legal_basis: Other Deceits under Article 318, paragraph 1 of the RPC requires (a) a false pretense, fraudulent act or pretense other than those in Articles 315 to 317; (b) made or executed prior to or simultaneously with the commission of the fraud; and (c) resulting damage or prejudice. Suppression of a material fact that one is bound in good faith to disclose is equivalent to a false representation, and the false statement must be the very cause or only motive for the complainant to part with his property. Judicial admissions made by a party during trial in the same case are conclusive and need no further proof, except when shown to have been made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made. (Spouses Llonillo v. People, G.R. No. 246787, January 30, 2024)
alac.application: (a) Hector admitted that the titles shown to him before the loan bore the bank mortgage annotation and that he saw it, so there was no suppression of the mortgage and it could not have induced him to part with his money. The second sangla-tira with Ivan was made a year after Hector's loan, so it was not a false pretense made prior to or simultaneously with the fraud. Hector's unpaid loan shows damage, but damage alone does not make the crime when the first two elements are missing. (b) Hector's claim on redirect does not show palpable mistake or that the admission was never made, so his categorical admission on cross-examination stands.
alac.conclusion: Fely and Gino must be acquitted of Other Deceits, though Hector may still recover the unpaid loan as a contractual obligation.

notes: The main opinion ends at "SO ORDERED." (about 48,600 characters of the roughly 252,000-character source text); the rest is footnotes and several separate opinions (concurring, dissenting, and concurring and dissenting), none of which was used. The Court summed up the petitioners' issues into two (jurisdiction and guilt); issue 3 is the question the Court itself posed when it took up civil liability. The Supreme Court's fallo awards only the PHP 300,000.00 principal with interest; it does not mention the MeTC's PHP 30,000.00 attorney's fees, and the Decision does not discuss them.
